planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in rocky, alkaline, well-drained limestone soil in full sun; reduce irrigation after the first two seasons once roots are established.

directions: Native to limestone canyons, rocky slopes, and caliche outcrops of the Edwards Plateau, Blackland Prairie, and Cross Timbers of central and north Texas, with outlying populations in Oklahoma and Arkansas, Texas ash is a compact, round-headed shade tree that stays well below the eventual size of white or green ash, making it a better fit for smaller residential lots. It is among the most drought- and alkaline-soil-tolerant of the native ashes, thriving on thin, rocky soils where irrigation-dependent shade trees struggle, and it produces some of the best fall color of any Hill Country native tree, with individual trees turning clear yellow, burgundy-purple, or orange. Like all North American ash species it is vulnerable to the invasive emerald ash borer, so it is best planted only where regional monitoring or biocontrol programs are active; check with a county extension office before planting. Deer generally leave established trees alone, and the winged samaras feed songbirds through winter.

planting.note: Plant small container-grown trees in fall in sharply drained, rocky, limestone or igneous soil in full sun to light shade; Texas madrone resents root disturbance and transplants poorly once established, so choose a permanent, well-drained site from the start.

directions: Found on rocky limestone and igneous slopes of the Edwards Plateau, Trans-Pecos, and the Davis and Chisos Mountains, Texas madrone is prized above all for its exfoliating bark, which peels away in thin curls to reveal smooth trunk and limb wood that shifts from chalky white through pink, cinnamon, and deep red as it weathers. Clusters of small, urn-shaped white flowers open in early spring and are followed by orange-red berries that draw mockingbirds, robins, and other fruit-eating birds. It is notoriously difficult to establish in cultivation, demanding sharp drainage, low fertility, and minimal supplemental water once past its first two years — richer garden soil or regular irrigation quickly kills it with root rot. Best sited on a rocky slope or berm where water never stands, ideally among the limestone-loving oaks and junipers it grows with in the wild.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in rocky, alkaline, well-drained limestone soil in full sun to part shade; establishes slowly and needs little supplemental water once past its first year.

directions: Endemic to limestone canyons, bluffs, and rocky slopes of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos, Lindheimer's silktassel is a dense, evergreen shrub named for German-Texan botanist Ferdinand Lindheimer, who catalogued much of the region's flora in the 1800s. Leathery, gray-green, holly-textured leaves persist year-round, and in late winter male plants produce pendulous, silvery-gray catkins — the namesake 'silk tassels' — several inches long, making this a dioecious species in which only male plants flower showily while females set small purple-brown fruit favored by birds. It is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established, thriving in the same thin, rocky, alkaline soils as Ashe juniper and Texas persimmon, and works well as an evergreen screen or backdrop shrub in a Hill Country xeriscape planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in rocky, well-drained limestone soil in full sun to part shade; this variety tolerates far less supplemental water than typical eastern black cherry once established.

directions: Restricted to the limestone canyons, bluffs, and dry slopes of the Edwards Plateau and Balcones Escarpment, escarpment black cherry is a shrubby, multi-trunked small tree markedly different in stature from the tall forest-form black cherry of the eastern United States. Smaller, thicker, more leathery leaves and a lower, rounder habit adapt it to the shallow, rocky, alkaline soils and intense summer heat of the Hill Country, where it needs only a fraction of the water that eastern black cherry requires. Clusters of small white flowers in spring give way to small dark cherries that ripen through summer, drawing mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds, while deer and small mammals browse the foliage. As with all Prunus serotina varieties, wilted leaves and seed pits contain cyanogenic compounds and should be kept from livestock, though the ripe fruit itself is edible and has traditionally been used for jellies and wine.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in extremely well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Compacta needs excellent drainage and will decline in heavy or waterlogged clay.

directions: Compacta is the dwarf-habit cultivar of cenizo (Leucophyllum frutescens, Texas sage), bred down to a dense 3-to-4-foot mound that fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and small borders where the sprawling 6-to-8-foot species would quickly overgrow the space. It retains the same soft, felted, silver-gray foliage and the species' signature 'barometer bush' habit of erupting into a flush of lavender-purple, bell-shaped flowers in the day or two following a rise in humidity or a summer rain, repeating the cycle from late spring through fall. Native to the caliche and limestone soils of the Edwards Plateau and Chihuahuan Desert, it is extremely heat and drought tolerant once established and is intolerant of rich, moist, or poorly drained soil, where root rot quickly sets in. An excellent low-water, low-maintenance shrub for xeric foundation plantings and rock gardens in zones 7 through 10.
